title: Ragtime records growing up and the shift to jazz; disclaims expertise
summary: He recalls ragtime records on the phonograph, the Tuxedo Band playing ragtime until about 1920, and the term jazz arriving. He cannot say how they differ and defers to Souchon and Menville.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: What we played: tunes and repertoire in the early days

blocks.x: as a kid growing up, we had, what was known as ragtime. We had ragtime records on the phonograph, along with Carusos and other Red Fields. But the transition of ragtime into jazz took place, I believe, back during my college days, back in the 1921-22 period. Now, you realize you're talking to a non-expert on jazz, and I'm only giving you a recollection that may not be authentic. Well, you say when you were going to high school, when you were going to dance or... Well, I wasn't much of a party boy

during my high school days. I would say what was played in those days was the mainly was what we call still called ragtime. It was I can remember the Tuxedo Band was a famous band. And they played what was genuinely called ragtime all the way down until I think about the 20. That's when the term jazz came into the picture. And just how jazz differed from ragtime as a non-expert, certainly I'm not in a position to tell you. I get that from Fouchon and my Lenville and that group. But I would say that in the evolution of this thing. You know those bands and I like to pat my foot to the music. But I have never the music has never played an important part in my, what shall we say, musical experience. But I've never been opposed. I've never been opposed to it, as I one is opposed to Mr. E.
